podcast.body: In a study at New York University, "My Sharona" was rated very low by students exhibiting psychopathic traits. The study examined the correlation between musical taste and psychopathy, indicating this song was disliked by those trending psychopathic. "These same people rated songs like Money for Nothing by Dire Straits, and the next My Shirona really low, same thing with classical music they didn't like it."

podcast.body: This song, arguably the "Nickelback of their day," was both loved and loathed by rock fans in 1979. It was loathed for being rock's first big number one in a year dominated by disco and for its "faux Beatles imagery and sexist lyrics." Despite the controversy, it sold millions and topped the Hot 100 for six weeks, defeating two Donna Summer number ones and Chic's "Le Freak." It remained popular with Generation Xers, making a comeback in the 90s film "Reality Bites," and inspired Weird Al Yankovic. "Amid all the hubbub, My Sharona sold millions and topped the Hot 100 for six weeks, defeating two Donna Summer Number ones and Sheik's Le Freak for the year and title."

podcast.body: This song, released in the summer of 1979, was a ubiquitous pop hit, characteristic of the emerging new wave and power pop genres. Its lyrics, which some found "creepy" even at the time, describe lead singer Doug Fieger's infatuation with Sharona Alperin, who was 17 when he (25) first saw her and 19 when they began dating. Fieger claimed he wrote it from the perspective of a 14-year-old boy. The song's enduring appeal, according to Billy Joel, lies not primarily in its "pubescent dumbbo words" but in its opening guitar riff, drum hook, and bouncy beat. "Never gonna stop, give it up, such a dirty mind. Always get it up for the touch of the younger kind."
